answers.java_tx_design: I redesigned the transaction boundary on our accounts service two years ago. It originally wrapped a balance update and an external KYC-check call in the same transaction, which meant a slow third-party KYC response — sometimes 3-4 seconds — held a row lock on the account the whole time. Under load that caused timeouts on unrelated balance reads for the same account. I moved the KYC call outside the transaction, using a pending-state flag that gets cleared once the check returns, which cut those lock-related timeouts from a few dozen a day to essentially zero. The failure that got me there: my first attempt just made the KYC call async without the pending flag, and a couple of accounts briefly showed a balance that hadn't actually cleared checks yet, which we had to roll back and rethink.
answers.java_ops: We had connection pool exhaustion on the accounts service during a marketing-driven signup spike — pool maxed at 25 connections while a slow onboarding query, unindexed on a new filter column, held connections for 6-7 seconds each. I found it from HikariCP's pool metrics showing wait times spiking past a minute, added the missing index, which got that query down to under 100ms, and bumped the pool to 40 as a buffer. Wait times went back to near zero within the same deploy, and I kept an eye on the pool dashboard daily for about a week to be sure it held under the next spike.
answers.rust_readiness: No production Rust yet. I've worked through the book and built a small tool that parses and validates our IBAN formats as a side project, mostly to get comfortable with ownership and error handling outside of exceptions. That took about a month of evenings. For anything closer to production I'd want at least a few months more before I'd trust my own judgment on a live path, and I'd want to start with something narrow and stateless rather than anything touching balances directly, measuring it against the existing Java version before relying on it.
answers.rust_boundary: I'd start with a piece that's pure computation, not persistence — something like fee calculation or IBAN validation — running it alongside the Java version and comparing outputs before trusting it for real traffic. I'd watch latency and memory before and after, plus a period of side-by-side output comparison rather than a straight cutover. I haven't carved out a language boundary myself before, so this is more my reasoning about how I'd approach it than a real example.
answers.money_correctness: At my company, duplicate delivery is generally handled through an idempotency key attached to each request, checked against a store before the write goes through, and retries use backoff so we're not hammering things. When numbers do drift, the principle is to correct with a new entry rather than editing the original, so there's a clean audit trail. I haven't personally led the fix on a case like that — it's sat more with our payments team than with me directly.
answers.incident_response: The KYC lock-contention issue I mentioned did become a real incident once — enough accounts hit timeouts that support started getting tickets. I don't remember the exact numbers on how many accounts were affected, but it was resolved within the same day once we identified the lock as the cause. The postmortem's outcome was the pending-flag redesign I described, and I don't recall us tracking afterward whether it fully prevented a repeat.
answers.process_skipping: During that KYC incident I didn't skip review — even under pressure, I got a teammate to glance at the pending-flag change before it went out, maybe a ten-minute delay. We do have an agreed exception for one-line config rollbacks during a declared incident, but that's a team-agreed exception, not something I decide alone in the moment.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I told my team lead about my first, incomplete fix attempt on the KYC issue the same day I realized it was wrong, rather than quietly patching it again and hoping nobody noticed. I've been on the on-call rotation for about three years now, roughly one week in five, and I mentor one junior engineer on the team, mostly pairing through their first few production incidents so they're not facing one alone the first time.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a proposal to add a Redis cache in front of the accounts balance read path. I benchmarked our actual read latency under realistic load and it was already well within our target, so the cache would've added consistency risk for no real gain. The team agreed to drop it after seeing the numbers, and once decided, I didn't keep raising it in later planning meetings.
answers.own_contribution: On the KYC transaction-boundary fix: identifying the lock contention and designing the pending-flag approach were mine; the decision to roll it out gradually, account-tier by account-tier, was a joint call with my product manager to limit blast radius. On the caching disagreement, the benchmark was mine alone; the decision to drop the idea was the team's, made together once everyone had seen the same numbers.
answers.java_recovery: After a batch job that computes daily interest accruals stopped partway through due to an OOM, I scoped the impact with a query comparing accounts that should have an accrual entry for that date against ones that actually did, which found about 1,400 missing entries. I fixed it by rerunning the accrual calculation just for those accounts and inserting the missing entries with that date, rather than backdating a full rerun, then cross-checked total accrued interest against our finance team's expected daily total before calling it resolved.
answers.java_perf_change: I brought p99 latency on the account balance endpoint down from about 900ms to 210ms by finding we were recalculating the full transaction history on every read instead of using a maintained running balance. I added a running-balance column updated transactionally alongside each write, which meant reads no longer touched transaction history at all in the common case. First attempt was adding a read-through cache instead, but balance changes were frequent enough that cache invalidation added more complexity than it saved, so I dropped that approach for the running-balance column instead.
answers.rust_hands_on: In the IBAN validation tool I mentioned, I got stuck trying to return a reference to a substring of the input while also modifying the input to normalize whitespace — the borrow checker wouldn't let me hold both. I ended up doing the normalization first into a new owned String, then slicing from that instead of trying to reference the original input while mutating it. Small thing, but it's the point where lifetimes stopped being an abstract rule and started being something I could reason about.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move our onboarding flow — it changes constantly as compliance requirements shift, and none of us are fast enough in Rust yet to keep up with that pace of change. I haven't held back an actual rewrite myself, but I did argue against a full rewrite of the accounts service in a newer Java framework a while back, on the grounds that the risk wasn't worth the marginal benefit, and the team agreed to upgrade incrementally instead.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: In general, the kind of reconciliation mismatch I've seen discussed at my company usually comes down to a timezone boundary at day cutover, a rounding difference between two systems, or a refund arriving after a period closed. The principle is always to fix it with a new correcting entry, not by editing the closed period. I haven't personally run an investigation like that end to end, though — it's typically been our finance engineering team's territory rather than mine.
answers.prod_data_verification: I try to avoid checking things against real balances directly. If something can't be reproduced in staging, my instinct is to use a masked copy of production-shaped data or a read-only comparison against the real path rather than touching live data. I haven't personally had to make that call under real pressure, so I can't give you a specific example of having done it myself.
